questions.stem: A client has persistent fear of being scrutinized or negatively judged in social situations, avoids eating or speaking in front of others, and the fear interferes with daily functioning. Which condition best fits this pattern?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Social anxiety disorder, with persistent fear of scrutiny or negative evaluation in social situations","B":"Generalized anxiety disorder, with excessive worry across many domains rather than social scrutiny","C":"Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with intrusive obsessions and compulsions rather than social fear","D":"Antisocial personality disorder, with disregard for others rather than fear of negative judgment"}}
questions.rationale: NIMH describes social anxiety disorder as fear or anxiety in situations where a person may be scrutinized, evaluated, or judged by others, often producing avoidance and functional impairment. Eating in front of others and public speaking are specifically cited examples.
questions.source_name: NIMH — Social Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know
questions.source_detail: Definition and signs/symptoms: fear of scrutiny, evaluation, judgment, embarrassment or rejection; avoidance; interference with daily life.

questions.stem: A client with influenza asks about the importance of antiviral timing. Which teaching is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Start as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours; later treatment may still help selected high-risk patients","B":"Wait until at least 48 hours have passed because early antiviral treatment provides less clinical benefit","C":"Delay treatment until influenza symptoms are nearly resolved so medication adverse effects are minimized","D":"Use timing only for dosing convenience because treatment benefit is unrelated to symptom duration"}}
questions.rationale: CDC 2026 guidance states that influenza antiviral treatment provides the greatest benefit when started early, especially within 48 hours. However, treatment can still provide benefit after 48 hours in hospitalized patients, patients with severe or progressive illness, and people at increased risk for complications.
questions.source_name: CDC — Influenza Antiviral Medications: Summary for Clinicians
questions.source_detail: Updated March 10, 2026: benefit greatest when started early, especially within 48 hours; later treatment can still benefit hospitalized/severe/progressive/high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A client with prior liver disease is receiving systemic fluconazole and develops rising aminotransferases. What should the nurse recognize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recognize possible hepatic toxicity and monitor worsening liver injury when liver tests become abnormal","B":"Assume fluconazole has no important hepatic effects even when the client's liver tests are rising","C":"Ignore abnormal liver tests unless blood glucose is also elevated during the antifungal treatment course","D":"Assume liver injury occurs only after a predictable cumulative dose and cannot occur earlier in therapy"}}
questions.rationale: Fluconazole labeling warns of rare serious hepatic toxicity and advises caution in patients with liver dysfunction. Patients who develop abnormal liver function tests during therapy should be monitored for more severe hepatic injury, and the drug should be discontinued if clinical signs or symptoms of liver disease attributable to fluconazole develop.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Fluconazole prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Warnings, Hepatic Injury: caution with liver dysfunction; monitor patients with abnormal liver function tests for more severe hepatic injury.

questions.stem: A client is receiving intravenous ferumoxytol for iron-deficiency anemia. Which safety measure is required by the current product label?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Observe during infusion and for at least 30 minutes afterward, with anaphylaxis treatment available","B":"Skip observation after infusion when a previous dose was tolerated without any adverse reaction","C":"Give the entire dose by rapid IV push because faster administration lowers hypersensitivity risk","D":"Monitor only for hypoglycemia because serious hypersensitivity is not a labeled ferumoxytol risk"}}
questions.rationale: Feraheme (ferumoxytol) carries a boxed warning for serious hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis. The May 31, 2026 label requires administration as an IV infusion over at least 15 minutes with personnel and therapies available to treat anaphylaxis, and observation during and for at least 30 minutes after the infusion.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Feraheme (ferumoxytol) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Updated May 31, 2026; Boxed Warning and section 5.1 Serious Hypersensitivity Reactions: infusion over at least 15 minutes; observe during and at least 30 minutes afterward.

questions.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is switched from warfarin to apixaban and asks whether INR testing will be used routinely to adjust the apixaban dose. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Do not routinely titrate apixaban to an INR; use the labeled indication and patient-specific criteria","B":"Use the same routine INR target and dose-adjustment strategy that is used for warfarin therapy","C":"Hold apixaban whenever INR is below 2.0 because a low INR indicates inadequate anticoagulation","D":"Skip clinical and laboratory follow-up because apixaban never requires medication safety monitoring"}}
questions.rationale: Apixaban has fixed labeled dosing schemes based on indication and specified patient factors rather than routine INR-guided titration. Clinical follow-up, renal/hepatic assessment when appropriate, adherence review, and bleeding surveillance remain important; the absence of routine INR dose adjustment does not mean monitoring is unnecessary.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — ELIQUIS (apixaban) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Dosage and Administration section 2.1: indication-specific fixed dosing and NVAF dose-reduction criteria; INR-based titration is not part of labeled apixaban dosing.

questions.stem: A client taking dabigatran has life-threatening, uncontrolled bleeding. Which specific reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Idarucizumab (Praxbind), the specific reversal agent for dabigatran anticoagulation","B":"Protamine sulfate injection, the specific reversal agent used for unfractionated heparin","C":"Phytonadione (vitamin K1), the reversal treatment for vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation","D":"Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab), the specific antidote used for severe digoxin toxicity"}}
questions.rationale: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) is a specific reversal agent for dabigatran and is indicated when reversal of dabigatran's anticoagulant effect is needed for emergency surgery/urgent procedures or life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding. Protamine reverses heparin, vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonists, and naloxone reverses opioids.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — PRAXBIND (idarucizumab) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Indications and Usage: reversal of dabigatran anticoagulant effects for emergency surgery/urgent procedures or life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding.

questions.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is prescribed apixaban. Which statement about the labeled adult dose-reduction criteria is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two labeled NVAF dose-reduction criteria are present","B":"Reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily whenever any degree of renal impairment is documented clinically","C":"Keep the dose unchanged because age, weight, and serum creatinine never affect NVAF dosing","D":"Increase the dose whenever serum creatinine reaches 1.5 mg/dL because renal clearance is lower"}}
questions.rationale: For stroke and systemic embolism prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, the current ELIQUIS label recommends 5 mg twice daily for most adults and 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of three criteria are present: age at least 80 years, body weight at most 60 kg, or serum creatinine at least 1.5 mg/dL. The prior item was too broad because apixaban dosing is indication-specific and renal impairment alone is not the universal rule described there.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — ELIQUIS (apixaban) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Current label version 38, section 2.1: NVAF dose 5 mg twice daily; reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of age ≥80 years, body weight ≤60 kg, or serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL are present.

questions.stem: A client hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF is being considered for initiation of an evidence-based beta-blocker. When is initiation most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Initiate after clinical stabilization, before discharge when appropriate, rather than during instability","B":"Start immediately at a full target dose while marked low-output or hemodynamic instability persists","C":"Avoid permanently because beta-blockers are contraindicated in every patient with chronic HFrEF","D":"Use only after all other guideline-directed therapies have been permanently discontinued first"}}
questions.rationale: Guideline-directed beta-blockers are foundational therapy for HFrEF. In hospitalized patients, initiation is appropriate after clinical stabilization and before discharge when feasible. Existing beta-blocker therapy is generally continued unless clinical circumstances such as marked volume overload, marginal low output, or other intolerance require adjustment. The prior wording incorrectly implied that beta-blockers are broadly avoided throughout acute decompensation.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC/HFSA — 2022 Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
questions.source_detail: Hospitalized HFrEF guidance: initiate guideline-directed therapy after clinical stability is achieved; beta-blocker initiation before discharge is reasonable once stabilized, while dose reduction/withholding may be considered with marked volume overload or marginal low output.

questions.stem: A client has severe digoxin toxicity with a life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab), which binds circulating digoxin during severe toxicity","B":"Protamine sulfate injection, which neutralizes unfractionated heparin anticoagulant activity","C":"Phytonadione (vitamin K1), which reverses vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant effects","D":"Flumazenil injection, which reverses selected benzodiazepine sedative medication effects"}}
questions.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab binds digoxin and is indicated for life-threatening or potentially life-threatening digoxin toxicity, including serious ventricular arrhythmias. The other agents reverse different drug classes.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — DIGIFAB (digoxin immune Fab) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Indications and Usage: treatment of life-threatening or potentially life-threatening digoxin toxicity, including severe ventricular arrhythmias and other specified manifestations.

questions.stem: An adult client is prescribed insulin degludec (TRESIBA) once daily and asks whether every dose must be given at exactly the same clock time. Which teaching is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Adults may inject once daily at any time of day while following prescribed missed-dose instructions","B":"Adults must inject at exactly the same time each day or the basal insulin becomes unsafe to use","C":"TRESIBA is a rapid-acting mealtime insulin that should be administered before every meal","D":"Adults and children should both vary injection time freely from day to day without a schedule"}}
questions.rationale: The current TRESIBA label states that adults inject once daily at any time of day, while pediatric patients should inject once daily at the same time every day. Adult timing flexibility therefore should not be generalized to pediatric dosing.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — TRESIBA (insulin degludec) prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Section 2.2 General Dosing Instructions: adults inject once daily at any time of day; pediatric patients inject once daily at the same time every day.

questions.stem: Before giving sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain, the nurse learns that the client recently used sildenafil. Why is this important?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The combination can cause severe hypotension, syncope, or myocardial ischemia and is contraindicated","B":"Sildenafil blocks nitroglycerin absorption but does not create an important hemodynamic interaction","C":"The combination is recommended because additive vasodilation safely improves nitrate effectiveness","D":"No clinically important interaction exists between nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors"}}
questions.rationale: Current nitroglycerin labeling contraindicates use in patients taking PDE-5 inhibitors including sildenafil because concomitant use can cause severe hypotension, syncope, or myocardial ischemia.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Nitroglycerin Sublingual Tablets prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Section 4.1 PDE-5 Inhibitors and sGC Stimulators: do not use with sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, or avanafil; severe hypotension, syncope, or myocardial ischemia can occur.

questions.stem: During central venous catheter insertion, why should the nurse use a standardized insertion checklist that includes hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions, and appropriate chlorhexidine skin antisepsis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Promote consistent use of evidence-based measures that reduce central-line bloodstream infection risk","B":"Replace sterile technique whenever the clinician inserting the central line has extensive experience","C":"Eliminate the need to assess daily whether the central venous catheter remains clinically necessary","D":"Permit individual infection-prevention steps to be skipped whenever venous access appears easy"}}
questions.rationale: CDC central-line prevention recommendations include hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions for insertion, chlorhexidine-based skin preparation, and appropriate catheter-site practices. A checklist supports reliable implementation but does not replace sterile technique or ongoing review of line necessity.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections
questions.source_detail: Summary recommendations: hand hygiene; maximal sterile barrier precautions during CVC insertion; chlorhexidine skin preparation; prompt removal of catheters no longer essential.

questions.stem: A reusable surgical instrument is heavily soiled with blood and tissue during a procedure. Which point-of-use practice best supports effective later reprocessing?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Follow validated point-of-use instructions and prevent gross soil from drying before full reprocessing","B":"Allow blood and tissue to dry completely because dried debris improves sterilant penetration later","C":"Skip cleaning when terminal sterilization is planned because sterilization reliably removes all soil","D":"Apply any available chemical regardless of device instructions because all cleaning agents are equivalent"}}
questions.rationale: Effective sterilization depends on adequate cleaning. CDC guidance states that devices should be cleaned as soon as practical after use because dried soil makes removal more difficult and can interfere with disinfection or sterilization. Point-of-use handling should follow validated manufacturer instructions rather than improvised chemicals.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities
questions.source_detail: Cleaning section: clean medical devices as soon as practical after use because materials become dried onto instruments; cleaning is required before high-level disinfection and sterilization.

questions.stem: A nurse on a burn unit asks whether every patient with a serious burn automatically requires a special universal 'burn isolation' protocol beyond Standard and indicated Transmission-Based Precautions. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use Standard and indicated Transmission-Based Precautions, with burn-unit measures based on risk and policy","B":"Place every serious burn patient in airborne isolation regardless of infection status or procedure type","C":"Use no infection-prevention measures because burn wounds are not susceptible to colonization or infection","D":"Place every burn patient in a positive-pressure HEPA room regardless of transplant status or fungal risk"}}
questions.rationale: Serious burns disrupt skin integrity and infection prevention is important, but the prior item overstated a universal 'stricter isolation' approach. CDC's scientific review states that there is no consensus on the most effective special infection-control configuration for serious burn patients and no defined universal combination of barrier precautions. Standard Precautions and indicated Transmission-Based Precautions remain fundamental, with additional burn-unit practices based on risk and facility policy.
questions.source_name: CDC — Isolation Precautions Scientific Review: Burn Patients
questions.source_detail: Scientific review section on patients with serious burns: no consensus on the most effective special infection-control practices or barrier-precaution combination; evidence supports emphasis on hand hygiene and appropriate barriers for direct contact.

questions.stem: An allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipient is placed in a CDC-defined Protective Environment. What is the primary purpose of this environment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce allogeneic HSCT exposure to environmental fungi using engineering controls and indicated precautions","B":"Protect staff from the transplant recipient by replacing Standard Precautions with reverse isolation","C":"Eliminate the need for hand hygiene and personal protective equipment during transplant recipient care","D":"Use the same protective room configuration for every immunocompromised patient regardless of condition"}}
questions.rationale: CDC's Protective Environment is specifically recommended for allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant patients to reduce exposure to environmental fungi using engineering controls such as HEPA filtration and positive pressure. It does not replace Standard or Transmission-Based Precautions and should not be generalized to every immunocompromised patient.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Protective Environment
questions.source_detail: Protective Environment recommendations: use for allogeneic HSCT patients to reduce environmental fungal exposure; maintain Standard and Transmission-Based Precautions as indicated.

questions.stem: Why does a hospital need a water management program that includes the building's internal plumbing rather than focusing only on outdoor fountains or cooling towers?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Legionella can grow in complex building water systems, and healthcare patients may be highly vulnerable","B":"Legionella is limited to outdoor fountains and cooling towers and does not grow in indoor plumbing","C":"Municipal treatment guarantees Legionella cannot multiply after water enters the healthcare building","D":"Water management programs address taste and odor only and are unrelated to Legionella prevention"}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends comprehensive water management programs for healthcare facilities because complex building water systems can support Legionella growth and transmission and healthcare facilities serve vulnerable populations. Water management therefore includes internal plumbing and relevant devices, not only outdoor water features.
questions.source_name: CDC — Water Management in Healthcare Facilities
questions.source_detail: March 15, 2024: healthcare facilities should develop and implement comprehensive water management programs to reduce Legionella growth and transmission; building water systems and vulnerable populations are central risk considerations.

questions.stem: A hospital receives an FDA medical-device recall notice for equipment currently in use. What is the most appropriate initial facility response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identify affected devices and follow recall-specific correction or removal instructions and facility policy","B":"Discard every recalled device permanently because all FDA recalls require product removal or destruction","C":"Continue using every recalled device until it fails because recall notices are informational only","D":"Ignore the recall unless a patient has already been injured by the exact affected device in use"}}
questions.rationale: FDA defines a medical-device recall as a correction or removal action. A recall does not always require stopping use or returning the device; some recalls require inspection, adjustment, repair, labeling changes, or other correction. The facility should identify affected inventory and follow the specific recall instructions and its internal response process.
questions.source_name: FDA — What Is a Medical Device Recall?
questions.source_detail: Current FDA page: a recall may involve correction or removal; it does not always mean the product must be stopped or returned and can require checking, adjusting, or fixing the device.

questions.stem: Which instruction is part of respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette in a healthcare setting?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cover the mouth and nose, dispose of used tissues, and clean hands after respiratory secretions","B":"Cough openly when symptoms are mild because source-control measures are unnecessary in that setting","C":"Reuse contaminated tissues during the visit because repeated use reduces unnecessary waste","D":"Skip hand hygiene after coughing or sneezing whenever a disposable tissue was used correctly"}}
questions.rationale: CDC includes respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette within Standard Precautions. Symptomatic people should contain respiratory secretions by covering the mouth and nose, use and dispose of tissues, and clean their hands after contact with respiratory secretions.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Respiratory Hygiene/Cough Etiquette
questions.source_detail: Summary Recommendations IV.C.2.a and Appendix A Table 4: cover mouth/nose when coughing or sneezing, use/dispose tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.

questions.stem: A hospital is considering reprocessing a device originally labeled for single use. Which statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Some single-use devices may be reprocessed, but the reprocessor must meet applicable FDA requirements","B":"Every single-use device may be reprocessed without validation, labeling review, or regulatory oversight","C":"FDA prohibits reprocessing every device labeled for single use regardless of device or process","D":"Hospital reprocessors are exempt from manufacturer-type FDA requirements for quality and safety"}}
questions.rationale: FDA states that not all single-use devices are suitable for reprocessing, but some can be shown safe and effective through validated reprocessing. Third-party and hospital reprocessors are regulated as manufacturers and must meet applicable premarket, labeling, quality-system, and postmarket requirements.
questions.source_name: FDA — Reprocessing Single-Use Medical Devices: Information for Health Care Facilities
questions.source_detail: Current FDA guidance: not all SUDs are suitable for reprocessing; certain SUDs may be demonstrated safe/effective through validation; healthcare-facility reprocessors are subject to applicable manufacturer requirements.

questions.stem: Why do nurse staffing committees include direct-care nurse representation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Incorporate frontline knowledge of patient acuity, care needs, and staff skills into staffing plans","B":"Exclude direct-care nurses from staffing decisions so planning remains entirely administrative","C":"Use one fixed staffing number for every shift without considering acuity, workload, or skill mix","D":"Transfer staffing decisions to personnel with no direct knowledge of unit-level patient-care demands"}}
questions.rationale: ANA describes staffing committees as nurse-led groups that create unit-level staffing plans based on patient acuity and needs matched with staff skills and experience, and supports substantial direct-care nurse representation. Frontline input is therefore an intended safety feature of this model.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Advocating for Safe Staffing in Nursing
questions.source_detail: Staffing committees: nurse-led groups create unit-level staffing plans based on patient population acuity/needs and staff skills/experience; ANA supports direct-care nurse representation.

questions.stem: A fire starts inside a hospital and threatens a patient-care area. Which principle should guide the unit's response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Activate the facility fire plan, including alarm, relocation or evacuation, and assigned staff duties","B":"Use an improvised response because written emergency procedures are unnecessary during hospital fires","C":"Wait for the fire to spread before beginning evacuation or activating the facility emergency plan","D":"Treat the incident only as an external mass-casualty influx and ignore internal fire procedures"}}
questions.rationale: The prior item relied on a loose 'internal versus external disaster' label. OSHA hospital fire-safety guidance instead supports a concrete emergency-action-plan response: reporting/alarm procedures, evacuation or escape routes, assigned duties, and trained personnel. CMS emergency preparedness likewise uses an all-hazards approach that includes fires and loss of facility operations.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Hospitals: Fire Safety and Emergency Action Plans
questions.source_detail: Hospital fire-safety guidance requires applicable emergency action planning; 29 CFR 1910.38 plan elements include reporting fires, evacuation procedures/escape routes, critical-operation duties, accountability, rescue/medical duties, and responsible contacts.

questions.stem: A client and clinician are choosing among several reasonable treatments. What best describes shared decision making?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Clinician and client exchange evidence, risks, benefits, values, and goals and work toward a shared decision","B":"Clinician makes the decision alone and avoids discussing reasonable alternatives with the client","C":"Client receives no clinical guidance and must choose entirely alone among unfamiliar treatment options","D":"Process is appropriate only when exactly one treatment option exists and no preference is involved"}}
questions.rationale: AHRQ defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which patients and clinicians make decisions informed by evidence, clinician knowledge and experience, and the patient's values, goals, preferences, and circumstances.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — About Shared Decision Making
questions.source_detail: Current AHRQ definition: collaborative process involving evidence, care-team knowledge/experience, and patient values, goals, preferences and circumstances.

questions.stem: A client with complex chronic illness is assigned a professional case manager. Which activity is most consistent with case management practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Coordinate services and resources across settings to support client goals, continuity, and safe transitions","B":"Replace every other healthcare professional so one case manager provides all treatment and coordination","C":"Make medical decisions without client participation because coordination requires centralized authority","D":"Provide bedside procedures only and avoid communication with community and specialty care services"}}
questions.rationale: CMSA's Standards of Practice frame case management as a professional, client-centered process across the healthcare continuum. Coordination, communication, resource linkage, transitions, and advocacy are core functions rather than replacing other clinicians or excluding the client.
questions.source_name: Case Management Society of America — Standards of Case Management Practice
questions.source_detail: 2022 Standards of Practice with 2024 DEIB/Health Equity addendum; case-management process supports client-centered coordination and continuity across the healthcare continuum.

questions.stem: An adult with decision-making capacity understands the recommended inpatient treatment and its risks but insists on leaving the hospital. What is the best response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Respect informed refusal, document capacity and risks, and provide the safest feasible follow-up plan","B":"Physically detain the capable adult solely because the healthcare team believes leaving is unsafe","C":"Assume the decision to leave automatically proves lack of capacity and permits involuntary detention","D":"Use a signed AMA form as the only required step and omit discussion of risks and alternatives"}}
questions.rationale: A capable adult can refuse recommended treatment even when clinicians consider the choice unsafe. Informed refusal is a process rather than merely a signature: assess capacity, explain risks, benefits and alternatives, document the discussion, and reduce harm through a safe-as-feasible discharge/follow-up plan. Facility policy and applicable law still apply.
questions.source_name: AMA Journal of Ethics — Ethically Informed Discharge Planning and Informed Refusal
questions.source_detail: AMA ethics discussion: adults with decision-making capacity may refuse treatment; holding a capable patient may constitute false imprisonment. Informed refusal requires capacity assessment, information about consequences, and documentation rather than relying only on an AMA form.

questions.stem: A hospital uses a restraint for violent or self-destructive behavior in an adult. Which statement about the order is accurate under the federal hospital Conditions of Participation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use time-limited orders; an adult violent-behavior restraint order may renew for up to 4 hours","B":"Use one restraint order indefinitely as long as staff continue documenting ongoing agitation","C":"Write routine restraint orders for 30 days when violent or self-destructive behavior has occurred","D":"Use standing or PRN restraint orders whenever staff anticipate that violent behavior may recur"}}
questions.rationale: 42 CFR 482.13 requires restraint or seclusion for violent or self-destructive behavior to be ordered by an authorized practitioner and limits renewal periods by age. For adults age 18 or older, an order may be renewed up to 4 hours at a time, subject to the regulation's reassessment, monitoring, face-to-face evaluation, discontinuation, and state-law requirements. Standing or PRN restraint orders are not permitted.
questions.source_name: eCFR — 42 CFR §482.13, Condition of Participation: Patient's Rights
questions.source_detail: §482.13(e), restraint/seclusion: no standing or PRN orders; violent/self-destructive behavior renewal limits include 4 hours for adults age 18 or older, with continued monitoring and reassessment requirements.

questions.stem: A client agrees to receive care by telehealth. Which statement about informed consent is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Follow applicable state telehealth consent law and document required consent for the virtual encounter","B":"Assume informed consent never applies to telehealth because no in-person examination occurs there","C":"Apply one identical telehealth consent rule in every state because jurisdiction never changes requirements","D":"Leave the consent process entirely to the client without explaining what to expect from telehealth"}}
questions.rationale: HHS telehealth guidance states that official informed consent may be required and that specific consent laws vary by state. Clinicians should explain what patients can expect, address rights and privacy considerations, and ensure required consent is received and documented. The prior item was too broad in implying one universal telemedicine-consent rule.
questions.source_name: HHS Telehealth — Obtaining Informed Consent
questions.source_detail: Current federal telehealth guidance: specific informed-consent laws vary by state; explain what to expect and patient rights; receive and document required written, electronic, or verbal consent as applicable.

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly scheduled for prolonged work hours because of chronic staffing shortages. Which patient-safety concern is most supported by current ANA guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recognize fatigue from long hours and inadequate staffing as a safety risk that requires mitigation","B":"Treat fatigue only as a personal wellness issue with no meaningful relationship to patient safety","C":"Use extended mandatory overtime as the preferred long-term substitute for adequate staffing plans","D":"Discourage nurses from reporting fatigue because staffing concerns are unrelated to safety duties"}}
questions.rationale: ANA's position statement effective May 27, 2026 identifies nurse fatigue as a patient-safety and workforce-safety issue. It links long hours, heavy workload, inadequate staffing, and shiftwork with increased medical errors and calls for system-level strategies including appropriate staffing, realistic workloads, reasonable work hours, and contingency staffing plans. The item was reframed from a blanket legal claim about mandatory overtime to the supported fatigue/safety principle.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Addressing Nurse Fatigue to Promote Health, Safety, and Well-Being for All
questions.source_detail: ANA Position Statement, effective May 27, 2026: fatigue is a nurse and patient safety crisis; long hours, workload and inadequate staffing are linked to errors; employers and nurses share mitigation responsibilities.

questions.stem: An adult has fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, focal crackles, and no obvious alternative diagnosis. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect community-acquired pneumonia and obtain diagnostic evaluation, including imaging when indicated","B":"Diagnose allergic rhinitis from the findings and avoid further respiratory evaluation or imaging","C":"Assume bacterial pneumonia and identify the causative organism from symptoms alone without testing","D":"Treat the findings as a normal upper-respiratory illness that requires no additional assessment"}}
questions.rationale: Symptoms and focal lung findings can raise suspicion for community-acquired pneumonia, but clinical findings alone do not establish etiology. ATS/IDSA CAP guidance applies to adults with clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed pneumonia. The revised item therefore asks for suspicion and evaluation rather than claiming the symptom cluster alone confirms CAP.
questions.source_name: ATS/IDSA — Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-Acquired Pneumonia
questions.source_detail: Official ATS/IDSA guideline, published October 1, 2019 with additional resources updated through 2023; guideline management framework addresses clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed CAP.

questions.stem: A client has a cough lasting more than 3 weeks, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and hemoptysis. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect pulmonary tuberculosis, use appropriate airborne precautions, and arrange prompt TB evaluation","B":"Treat the symptoms as an uncomplicated common cold and postpone additional respiratory evaluation","C":"Assume seasonal allergies despite hemoptysis, prolonged cough, weight loss, and night sweats","D":"Delay diagnostic evaluation until the cough and systemic symptoms persist for several more months"}}
questions.rationale: CDC lists cough lasting 3 weeks or longer, hemoptysis, chest symptoms, unexplained weight loss, fever, and night sweats among pulmonary TB findings. Healthcare TB infection-control programs should ensure prompt detection and airborne infection-isolation precautions for confirmed or presumptive infectious TB disease.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Overview and Signs/Symptoms of Tuberculosis Disease
questions.source_detail: CDC 2024-2025 clinical guidance: pulmonary TB symptoms include cough ≥3 weeks, hemoptysis, weight loss and night sweats; healthcare settings require prompt detection and airborne infection isolation for confirmed or presumptive infectious TB.

questions.stem: A client with a soft-tissue infection develops rapidly progressive swelling, severe pain out of proportion to visible skin findings, high fever, and hypotension. What is the priority interpretation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect necrotizing fasciitis and obtain immediate surgical evaluation without unnecessary imaging delay","B":"Treat as uncomplicated cellulitis and wait for oral antibiotics to fail before escalating care","C":"Assume a benign allergic reaction because severe pain and hypotension are expected allergy findings","D":"Wait until extensive skin necrosis appears before considering a deep necrotizing soft-tissue infection"}}
questions.rationale: CDC describes pain out of proportion to local skin findings, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, bullae or necrosis as warning features of necrotizing fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency; imaging can assist in selected cases but should never delay surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Type II Necrotizing Fasciitis
questions.source_detail: Current CDC guidance: pain out of proportion, rapid progression and systemic findings heighten suspicion; imaging should never delay surgical exploration; prompt surgical management is essential.

questions.stem: A client develops unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness after prolonged travel. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate when lower-extremity DVT is suspected?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use validated pretest probability, then D-dimer and/or proximal or whole-leg ultrasound as indicated","B":"Diagnose DVT from unilateral swelling and tenderness alone without objective diagnostic testing","C":"Use a positive D-dimer alone to establish DVT in every patient regardless of pretest probability","D":"Rule out DVT when the patient can walk because preserved ambulation excludes venous thrombosis"}}
questions.rationale: ASH diagnostic guidelines use validated pretest probability to guide DVT testing. Low-probability patients can begin with a highly sensitive D-dimer followed by ultrasound when needed, while intermediate- or high-probability patients commonly require proximal or whole-leg ultrasonography. A positive D-dimer alone does not diagnose DVT. The prior item was corrected from the oversimplified instruction to obtain a 'Doppler ultrasound' based only on symptoms.
questions.source_name: American Society of Hematology — Guidelines for Diagnosis of Venous Thromboembolism
questions.source_detail: ASH 2018 VTE diagnosis guideline, reviewed by ASH in 2022 and retained for ongoing monitoring: lower-extremity DVT recommendations 5-8 use pretest probability with D-dimer and proximal/whole-leg ultrasonography; positive D-dimer alone is not diagnostic.

questions.stem: A client develops focal bone pain, warmth, swelling, and fever several weeks after a deep puncture wound to the foot. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cellulitis limited to superficial soft tissue without involvement of underlying bone","B":"Osteomyelitis caused by infection involving bone after the penetrating foot injury","C":"Deep vein thrombosis caused primarily by venous stasis from prolonged immobility","D":"Acute gout caused by urate crystal deposition in the first metatarsophalangeal joint"}}
questions.rationale: Penetrating trauma can directly inoculate organisms and lead to osteomyelitis. Focal bone pain with local warmth or swelling and systemic symptoms such as fever warrants evaluation for bone infection.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Osteomyelitis (StatPearls)
questions.source_detail: History and Physical; contiguous/direct-inoculation osteomyelitis after trauma; last update May 31, 2023; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A severely malnourished client begins nutritional support. Which laboratory pattern is most concerning for refeeding syndrome?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stable phosphate with isolated mild sodium elevation after feeding has been restarted","B":"Rising phosphate with concurrent increases in potassium and magnesium after feeding starts","C":"Falling phosphate with concurrent decreases in potassium and magnesium after feeding starts","D":"Stable potassium and magnesium with isolated mild calcium elevation after feeding starts"}}
questions.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is characterized by clinically important electrolyte shifts after calories are reintroduced, particularly hypophosphatemia and often hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. These abnormalities can cause serious cardiac and neurologic complications.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome
questions.source_detail: ASPEN consensus recommendations, Nutrition in Clinical Practice 2020; diagnostic/electrolyte framework for refeeding syndrome; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: An older adult has poor oral intake and possible dehydration. How should the nurse interpret skin turgor during the assessment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skin turgor is unrelated to hydration assessment and should never be examined clinically","B":"Skin turgor is more reliable in older adults because aging increases dermal elasticity","C":"Skin turgor alone is sufficient to rule out dehydration when recoil appears normal","D":"Skin turgor is less reliable in older adults because normal aging reduces skin elasticity"}}
questions.rationale: Age-related loss of skin elasticity makes skin turgor less reliable for assessing dehydration in older adults. Hydration assessment should incorporate additional findings rather than relying on turgor alone.
questions.source_name: Deißler et al. — Hydration Status Assessment in Older Patients (2023)
questions.source_detail: Review of hydration assessment in adults ≥65 years: reduced skin turgor and multiple other classic clinical signs lack sufficient diagnostic accuracy; skin turgor correlates with age more than hydration status.

questions.stem: A client has a serum sodium of 152 mEq/L with intense thirst, restlessness, and confusion. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypernatremia, commonly reflecting a relative free-water deficit and causing neurologic symptoms","B":"Hyponatremia, commonly reflecting excess free water and producing the measured sodium value","C":"Hyperkalemia, because potassium excess directly explains an elevated measured sodium level","D":"A normal sodium concentration, because symptoms are unrelated to the laboratory measurement"}}
questions.rationale: A sodium concentration above the usual reference range is hypernatremia. It commonly reflects water deficit relative to sodium and may produce thirst and neurologic manifestations such as restlessness or confusion.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus — Sodium Blood Test
questions.source_detail: High blood sodium (hypernatremia) and associated symptoms/causes; U.S. National Library of Medicine; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client's red blood cell count is clearly below the laboratory reference interval. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The finding is most consistent with polycythemia and excessive circulating red cell mass","B":"The finding can support evaluation for anemia and reduced oxygen-carrying red cell mass","C":"The finding confirms normal hematologic status without need for clinical correlation","D":"The finding specifically diagnoses iron deficiency without considering any other causes"}}
questions.rationale: A low RBC count can occur with anemia, but RBC count alone does not determine the cause. The result should be interpreted with hemoglobin, hematocrit, indices, symptoms, and clinical context.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus — Red Blood Cell (RBC) Count
questions.source_detail: Interpretation of low RBC count and anemia; U.S. National Library of Medicine; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with chest pain has an elevated CK-MB value. Which statement best reflects current cardiac biomarker practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CK-MB primarily evaluates renal filtration and has no recognized relationship to myocardium","B":"CK-MB is more cardiac-specific than troponin and should replace serial troponin testing","C":"CK-MB can indicate myocardial injury, but cardiac troponin is the preferred biomarker today","D":"CK-MB alone proves acute myocardial infarction regardless of symptoms, ECG, or serial testing"}}
questions.rationale: CK-MB may rise with myocardial injury, but current chest-pain guidance identifies cardiac troponin, especially high-sensitivity troponin, as the preferred biomarker for myocardial injury. Biomarkers require clinical and ECG correlation.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA — 2021 Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain
questions.source_detail: Biomarkers section: serial cardiac troponin I/T is preferred for myocardial injury; high-sensitivity troponin preferred; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Which routine urinalysis finding generally warrants further evaluation rather than being considered an expected normal result?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A urine sample that is clear to pale yellow without visible blood or unusual sediment","B":"Negative nitrite and leukocyte esterase results in a client without urinary symptoms","C":"A urine pH that falls within the laboratory's established physiologic reference interval","D":"Detectable protein or glucose that persists or is clinically significant on urine testing"}}
questions.rationale: Protein and glucose are not normally present in significant amounts in urine. Their presence can reflect renal, metabolic, or other conditions and should be interpreted in clinical context and confirmed as appropriate.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus — Urinalysis
questions.source_detail: Urinalysis components and abnormal substances including excess protein and glucose; U.S. National Library of Medicine; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client asks what a stool-based occult blood screening test does. Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It looks for blood not visible to the eye; a positive screening result needs follow-up evaluation","B":"It directly visualizes the entire colon and can remove suspicious polyps during the same test","C":"It confirms colorectal cancer by itself, so a positive result eliminates need for colonoscopy","D":"It measures serum tumor markers and is unrelated to blood that may be present in the stool"}}
questions.rationale: Stool blood tests detect occult blood and are screening tests, not definitive cancer diagnoses. A positive stool-based screening test requires follow-up colonoscopy to determine the source.
questions.source_name: USPSTF — Colorectal Cancer: Screening
questions.source_detail: Recommendation statement: stool-based screening tests and requirement for colonoscopy after abnormal stool-based results; current recommendation accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks how coagulation factors contribute to hemostasis after blood-vessel injury. Which response is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They act only after a clot is fully formed and function mainly to dissolve the existing fibrin mesh","B":"They activate in a sequence that generates fibrin and helps stabilize the developing platelet plug","C":"They are identical to platelets and therefore have no separate role in secondary hemostasis","D":"They prevent platelet adhesion and keep fibrin from forming at the site of vascular injury"}}
questions.rationale: Coagulation factors activate through coordinated pathways that culminate in thrombin generation and fibrin formation. Fibrin stabilizes the platelet plug and supports formation of a durable clot.
questions.source_name: NHLBI — How Blood Clots
questions.source_detail: Blood clotting process: clotting factors and fibrin stabilize the platelet plug; National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client asks why total protein and the albumin/globulin ratio were ordered. Which explanation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They are pulmonary-function measures used primarily to quantify ventilation and gas exchange","B":"They are cardiac-specific tests used primarily to diagnose acute myocardial injury and infarction","C":"They can contribute information about nutritional status and some liver, kidney, or protein disorders","D":"They directly measure long-term glycemic control in the same way as hemoglobin A1c testing"}}
questions.rationale: Total protein and the A/G ratio can aid evaluation of nutritional status and conditions affecting liver function, kidney protein loss, immune proteins, or other systemic processes. They are not cardiac-specific tests.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus — Total Protein and Albumin/Globulin (A/G) Ratio
questions.source_detail: Clinical uses and interpretation of total protein and A/G ratio; U.S. National Library of Medicine; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with a healing pressure injury asks why the dietitian emphasized adequate protein intake. Which explanation is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Protein intake has no relationship to healing because collagen formation does not require amino acids","B":"Protein is used only for skeletal muscle growth and has no meaningful role in wound repair","C":"Protein should be restricted for every client with a pressure injury regardless of other conditions","D":"Protein supports tissue repair and wound healing, and significant wounds can increase protein needs"}}
questions.rationale: Adequate protein supports tissue repair, immune function, and wound healing. Nutrition plans for pressure injuries should be individualized, including consideration of increased protein needs when clinically appropriate.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Preventing Pressure Ulcers in Hospitals
questions.source_detail: Nutrition component of pressure-injury prevention/care: nutritional assessment and protein/energy support for at-risk patients; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client with spinal cord injury has neurogenic bowel dysfunction. Which approach best reflects an effective bowel-management program?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use an individualized, consistent bowel routine designed to produce predictable and effective elimination","B":"Wait for constipation or incontinence to occur, then treat each episode without a planned routine","C":"Rely only on fluid intake and avoid scheduled bowel care, rectal methods, or prescribed medications","D":"Use the same bowel schedule for every spinal cord injury regardless of function or personal goals"}}
questions.rationale: Guidelines for neurogenic bowel after spinal cord injury recommend an individualized bowel program with a consistent schedule and interventions tailored to neurologic function, lifestyle, diet, fluids, and other needs.
questions.source_name: Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine — Neurogenic Bowel Dysfunction CPG
questions.source_detail: 2021 clinical practice guideline; Guiding Principles and Basic Bowel Management: predictable elimination and consistent individualized schedule; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client is positioned for a prolonged operative procedure. Which nursing action most directly reduces positioning-related pressure injury risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid padding because pressure redistribution devices can interfere with the sterile surgical field","B":"Pad vulnerable bony prominences, maintain alignment, and reassess positioning throughout the case","C":"Delay all positioning reassessment until the procedure ends unless the client can report discomfort","D":"Use extra-tight safety straps over bony areas so the client cannot shift during the procedure"}}
questions.rationale: Perioperative pressure-injury prevention includes proper positioning, pressure redistribution/padding for vulnerable areas, and ongoing reassessment. Immobility during surgery increases pressure-injury risk.
questions.source_name: AORN — Positioning and Perioperative Pressure Injury Guidance
questions.source_detail: 2026 positioning safety guidance: padding bony prominences, alignment, and continued reassessment; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: An older adult at risk for dehydration rarely reports feeling thirsty. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Restrict routine fluids to prevent overload even when there is no clinical reason for restriction","B":"Wait until the client requests a drink because thirst remains a dependable hydration signal with age","C":"Offer fluids regularly when not contraindicated and monitor intake instead of relying only on thirst","D":"Assess hydration only once daily because frequent intake monitoring does not affect dehydration risk"}}
questions.rationale: Older adults may not reliably increase fluid intake in response to thirst. When not contraindicated, proactive access and offering of fluids plus monitoring can help reduce dehydration risk.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Adult Dehydration (StatPearls)
questions.source_detail: Older adults are disproportionately affected by dehydration partly because of reduced thirst sensation and dependence/access factors; current chapter accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client is planning international travel and asks which vaccines are needed. What is the nurse's best recommendation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait until after arrival because travel vaccines are generally not useful when given before departure","B":"Assume routine childhood vaccines cover all destination-specific infections encountered abroad","C":"Use one universal travel-vaccine list because recommendations do not depend on itinerary or season","D":"Use destination- and itinerary-specific travel guidance and arrange a pretravel health consultation"}}
questions.rationale: Travel health recommendations depend on destination, itinerary, timing, activities, and individual health factors. CDC recommends pretravel assessment early enough to complete indicated vaccines and preventive measures.
questions.source_name: CDC Yellow Book 2026 — The Pre-Travel Consultation
questions.source_detail: Risk assessment based on traveler characteristics, itinerary, destination, and vaccine/prevention needs; 2026 edition; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A community health nurse is helping an employer plan worker safety education. What is a core purpose of effective safety training?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Teach workers to recognize workplace hazards and use the controls and safe practices required","B":"Replace engineering controls with education so employers no longer need to correct physical hazards","C":"Focus only on productivity because worker training has little relationship to injury prevention","D":"Limit hazard information to supervisors so frontline workers are not burdened with safety details"}}
questions.rationale: OSHA identifies education and training as a core element of safety and health programs. Workers need information and skills to recognize hazards, understand controls, and perform work safely.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Education and Training, Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs
questions.source_detail: Core element: train workers to identify hazards, understand controls, and work safely; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Which teaching point is appropriate for an adult who wants to improve sleep habits?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use bright electronic screens immediately before bed to strengthen the normal sleep response","B":"Keep a consistent sleep schedule, reduce evening screen exposure, and avoid late caffeine","C":"Vary bedtime by several hours each night so the body does not become dependent on a schedule","D":"Use caffeine in the evening because stimulant effects generally shorten sleep-onset latency"}}
questions.rationale: CDC sleep guidance recommends consistent sleep and wake times, turning off electronic devices before bed, and avoiding caffeine later in the day as practical habits that support better sleep.
questions.source_name: CDC — About Sleep
questions.source_detail: Better sleep habits section: consistent schedule, electronic devices off before bedtime, avoid afternoon/evening caffeine; May 15, 2024; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: After trauma, a client has significant gaps in memory for important autobiographical information that exceed ordinary forgetfulness. Which condition should be considered?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Malingering by definition, because any memory gap after trauma indicates intentional symptom production","B":"Normal forgetfulness because trauma cannot be associated with clinically important memory disruption","C":"A dissociative disorder involving disruption of memory that warrants further mental-health evaluation","D":"Antisocial personality disorder because autobiographical amnesia is a defining diagnostic feature"}}
questions.rationale: Dissociative disorders can involve disruption of memory and may be associated with trauma. A diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and exclusion of neurologic, substance-related, and other causes; the presentation should not be labeled malingering without evidence.
questions.source_name: Merck Manual Professional — Dissociative Amnesia
questions.source_detail: Clinical features: inability to recall important autobiographical information, often associated with trauma or stress, beyond ordinary forgetting; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Which description best characterizes the traditional DSM grouping of Cluster B personality disorders?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Primary neurocognitive decline with progressive memory loss as the defining feature of the cluster","B":"Odd or eccentric patterns, including paranoid and schizoid personality disorders in the cluster","C":"Anxious or fearful patterns, including avoidant and dependent personality disorders in the cluster","D":"Dramatic, emotional, or erratic patterns, including borderline and antisocial personality disorders"}}
questions.rationale: DSM-based teaching traditionally groups antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders in Cluster B, often summarized as dramatic, emotional, or erratic. Cluster labels are descriptive groupings, not substitutes for individual diagnostic criteria.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Personality Disorders (Nursing: Mental Health and Community Concepts)
questions.source_detail: Current NCBI nursing text accessed 2026-08-14: Cluster B includes antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders and is characterized by dramatic, overly emotional, or unpredictable thinking/behavior.
